lessons.culture: In Hejazi homes, removing shoes at the door is standard practice, especially in more traditional settings. Bringing a small gift when visiting shows respect without being ostentatious. Welcoming guests warmly with "hayyak allah" reflects the Hijaz's strong hosting tradition shaped by centuries of pilgrimage and trade. The phrase "laa takallaf" (don't trouble yourself) puts guests at ease and emphasizes the host's pleasure in their presence.

lessons.culture: Offering coffee and tea is a cornerstone of Hejazi hospitality, often served with dates or sweets. The Hejazi custom of asking "shinnu bitabgha tashrab" shows warm interest in the guest's preferences. Comments about children growing up are common and well-received in family visits. The phrase "al-jilsah" (gathering) reflects the importance of social time in Hejazi culture, where family and friends gather regularly.

lessons.culture: In Hejazi homes, food preparation is a point of pride and sharing recipes is common among women. The phrase "bil-hana wa-ash-shifa" (with happiness and healing) is the standard way to wish diners to enjoy their meal. Hejazi cooks often emphasize that dishes were made fresh that day, showing respect for guests. Generous portions are a sign of hospitality, and refusing politely without offense is an art in Hejazi culture.

lessons.culture: In Hejazi culture, goodbyes at the door often take a long time because hosts don't want guests to leave quickly. The phrase "don't forget, the house is always yours" expresses genuine warmth and an open-door policy. Checking on guests after they leave is considered caring behavior. Using "God willing" (inshallah) reflects both religious practice and practical acceptance that plans depend on circumstances.

challenge.title: Hosting or Visiting: A Full Exchange
challenge.instructions: Write a short conversation where you either welcome a guest into your home from the door to the table, or visit someone else's home and take your leave at the end. Use at least one greeting-at-the-door phrase, one phrase about food or drink, and one closing/thanking phrase.
required_elements: a welcome phrase at the door (e.g. 7ayyak allah / tfaddal daakhil)
an offer of food or drink (e.g. shinnu bitabgha tashrab)
a closing thanks or goodbye (e.g. allah ya3tiik al-3aafyah / ma3a as-salam)
